item.title: Next-gen privacy protocols: WireGuard vs OpenVPN vs Shadowsocks
item.description:
WireGuard, OpenVPN, and Shadowsocks often appear in the same privacy conversation, but they were built for different jobs. WireGuard strips VPN tunneling down to a compact modern design.

OpenVPN keeps the flexibility that made it a long-running enterprise standard. Shadowsocks approaches the problem from another direction, using an encrypted proxy architecture designed to make traffic harder to classify and block.

For IT teams, that difference matters more than a generic speed ranking. The right protocol depends on whether the priority is low overhead, compatibility, or resistance to network filtering.

WireGuard keeps the tunnel deliberately small

WireGuard became popular partly because of what it leaves out. Its original Linux implementation was designed to stay under roughly 4,000 lines of code, excluding cryptographic primitives. That is tiny compared with mature VPN stacks built around TLS libraries, multiple authentication systems, and years of backward-compatible options.

The benefit is easier review. A smaller security-sensitive codebase gives auditors less implementation logic to inspect and developers fewer moving parts to configure incorrectly. It does not guarantee that vulnerabilities will never appear, but it makes the protocol easier to reason about.

WireGuard is also intentionally opinionated about cryptography. Rather than negotiating among long lists of algorithms, it uses a fixed modern suite that includes Curve25519, ChaCha20 with Poly1305, BLAKE2s, and HKDF. 

That simplicity carries into performance. WireGuard runs over UDP, uses a short handshake, and was designed for efficient packet processing. Its ability to relearn a peer’s endpoint also makes it well suited to laptops and phones that move between Wi-Fi and cellular networks.

OpenVPN still earns its place in enterprise networks

OpenVPN is considerably more complex, but much of that complexity exists for a reason. Its TLS-based architecture supports certificates, certificate authorities, revocation, external authentication systems, TCP or UDP transport, and detailed routing policies. Administrators can fit it into infrastructure that was built long before WireGuard appeared.

A company with an established public key infrastructure may therefore value OpenVPN’s controls more than a smaller codebase.

Historically, that flexibility also came with more processing overhead. OpenVPN handled much of its data path in user space, while its TLS and crypto dependencies created a larger software surface than WireGuard’s fixed design.

That performance gap is no longer as simple as old benchmark charts suggest. OpenVPN 2.6 supports Data Channel Offload on Linux, Windows, and FreeBSD, moving packet-processing work into the kernel and improving throughput considerably. 

OpenVPN is best understood as a mature, configurable system rather than simply an older and slower WireGuard. Its extra machinery can be unnecessary for a personal VPN connection and useful for exactly the same reason in an enterprise deployment.

Shadowsocks solves a different security problem

Shadowsocks is not a conventional VPN protocol. It is an encrypted proxy originally created for networks where censorship and protocol blocking are part of the threat model. 

Instead of creating the same type of layer-3 tunnel as WireGuard, Shadowsocks forwards traffic through an encrypted proxy connection. Modern implementations commonly use authenticated encryption, while the protocol avoids many of the obvious fixed signatures associated with traditional VPN traffic.

This becomes useful when a network operator is actively looking for VPN connections rather than merely inspecting their contents. A conventional VPN may encrypt every byte perfectly and still be recognizable as VPN traffic. Firewalls can examine handshake structures, packet sizes, timing, transport behavior, and other characteristics even when they cannot read the payload.

Why obfuscation is becoming harder

Older filtering systems often relied heavily on simple protocol signatures. Modern traffic classifiers can work with behavior as well.

That creates an interesting problem for Shadowsocks. Traffic that looks like high-entropy random data can defeat basic signature matching, but on an aggressively monitored network, “unrecognized encrypted traffic” can itself become something worth flagging.

Published research (PDF) has shown that Shadowsocks deployments can be detected through a mixture of passive traffic analysis and active probing. OpenVPN has faced similar research, with classifiers identifying characteristic packet patterns even when the content itself remained encrypted. 

WireGuard vs OpenVPN vs Shadowsocks

The architectural differences become clearer when the three are compared by purpose rather than by marketing labels.

This is also why having multiple protocol options in one client can be useful. Toggle says its VPN client supports WireGuard and Shadowsocks, allowing users to choose between them based on connection conditions. These product claims were not independently tested for this article.

That does not mean every connection should layer both technologies or that one automatically fixes the weaknesses of the other. The useful part is having access to different approaches without rebuilding the networking setup from scratch.

Choosing a protocol by the problem in front of you

Protocol selection gets easier when it starts with the environment instead of a favorite benchmark.

  1. Choose WireGuard when efficiency is the priority. It is a strong fit for mobile devices, remote workers, gaming, and other situations where low overhead and quick reconnection matter.
  2. Keep OpenVPN where compatibility matters more. Existing certificate systems, TCP requirements, complex routing, and older enterprise infrastructure may justify the extra complexity.
  3. Use Shadowsocks when filtering is the main obstacle. Its proxy architecture is designed for networks where recognizable VPN traffic may be restricted.
  4. Test the actual route. Server distance, packet loss, firewall policy, and local filtering can matter more than theoretical protocol performance.
  5. Do not equate encryption with invisibility. A tunnel can protect packet contents while remaining easy for a network classifier to identify.

The best protocol depends on what the network is fighting

WireGuard changed VPN design by proving that a secure tunnel could be built with far less code and far fewer configuration choices. OpenVPN remains relevant because enterprise networks often need exactly the controls WireGuard intentionally avoids. Shadowsocks tackles another problem entirely: keeping an encrypted connection usable when the network itself is trying to identify and restrict it.

For IT professionals, there is no need to force those designs into a single winner.

WireGuard is the stronger default when speed, mobility, and a small attack surface lead the requirements. OpenVPN remains useful when authentication and compatibility dominate. Shadowsocks becomes valuable when detection and blocking are part of the network environment.

item.title: Transferring Unused IPv4 Addresses in Asia Pacific: The Complete APNIC Playbook
item.description:
If your network needs more IPv4 space in the Asia Pacific region, the transfer market is now the main way to get it.  Asia Pacific Network Information Centre (APNIC) became the first regional registry to run out of freely allocated IPv4 on 15 April 2011, according to the IPv4 address exhaustion record.

That makes APNIC’s transfer policy the rulebook for almost every new block in the region. APNIC’s own summary page lists the permitted transfer scenarios and little else.  This guide covers the rest: who qualifies, what the registry checks, how the workflow runs, what it costs and where deals tend to stall.

Key Takeaways

  1. Both sides of a transfer inside the APNIC region must be current APNIC account holders, and the smallest block you can transfer is a /24.
  2. Buyers must show a detailed plan to use the space within 24 months. Buyers who already hold IPv4 must also show past usage and compliance with APNIC policy.
  3. Addresses delegated from APNIC’s 103/8 free pool cannot be transferred for at least five years after the original delegation.
  4. The seller starts the transfer in MyAPNIC and the buyer has 30 days to acknowledge it, or the request is cancelled.
  5. Pre-approval lets a buyer clear the needs assessment before finding a seller.
  6. The recipient generally pays APNIC’s transfer fee before the Whois record is updated.

Why APNIC Allows IPv4 Transfers

The goal of the policy is simple. It moves IPv4 from organizations that no longer need it to organizations that do but can’t get it from the free pool, as set out in the APNIC Internet Number Resource Policies.

APNIC treats addresses as licensed for use rather than owned. So a transfer is really a change in who the registry recognizes as the holder, recorded in the APNIC Whois Database.  APNIC does not recognize transfers made outside its policy and can require those addresses to be returned.

The Five Transfer Scenarios

APNIC permits five transfer paths for unused IPv4 addresses and AS numbers. Some economies in the region run their own National Internet Registry (NIR) under APNIC, which is why several paths involve one.

The scenario changes who you deal with, not the core test. Each one still asks whether the seller is the rightful holder and whether the buyer can justify the space.

What APNIC Requires From the Buyer

The recipient must be a current APNIC account holder before anything can move. From there, the test depends on whether you already hold IPv4.

A first-time holder must show a detailed plan for using the transferred space within 24 months.  An existing holder needs that plan too, plus its past usage rate and evidence that it complied with APNIC policy on earlier delegations.

The plan has to be backed by real documents. APNIC’s general request rules say evidence can include network engineering plans, subnetting plans, topology and routing descriptions, equipment invoices and purchase orders. Estimates must be realistic and justifiable, and incomplete requests wait until the gaps are fixed.

What APNIC Requires From the Seller

The source must be the currently registered holder of the block and cannot be involved in any dispute over it. The space must sit in the range APNIC administers and be allocated or assigned to a current account holder.

Three limits catch sellers most often:

  • Minimum size. Nothing smaller than a /24 can be transferred.
  • The 103/8 lock. Space delegated from APNIC’s final 103/8 pool cannot move for at least five years after the original delegation. If the original reason for the request no longer applies during that time, the addresses go back to APNIC.
  • Loss of rights. Once the transfer completes, the seller has no further rights to the addresses, according to the APNIC Transfer Conditions.

If you are buying, check the delegation date of any 103/8 block before you sign anything. A block still inside its five-year window cannot be transferred at all.

How a Transfer Runs in MyAPNIC

Every in-region transfer is lodged through MyAPNIC, APNIC’s member portal. The sequence below follows APNIC’s IPv4 Transfer Guide.

  1. Get pre-approved (optional but smart). The buyer submits the Transfer Pre-approval form in MyAPNIC before finding a source. Once approved, any transfer within the approved size moves ahead without the buyer justifying need again.
  2. The seller initiates. The source account starts the transfer in MyAPNIC and selects the addresses to move.
  3. The buyer acknowledges. The recipient has 30 days to accept the transfer. Miss that window and the request is cancelled.
  4. APNIC evaluates. The registry checks the transfer against its IPv4 transfer criteria.
  5. Fees are paid and Whois updates. The recipient pays the transfer fee, then APNIC updates the registration in its Whois Database.

Pre-approval is the step most buyers underuse. Doing it first means the needs review is settled before money changes hands, so a signed deal is far less likely to stall.

Working With a Registered Broker

Most buyers don’t have a seller lined up, which is where brokers come in. APNIC keeps a page of registered IPv4 brokers that have signed an agreement to follow its broker guidelines, including acting in good faith with both sides. 

APNIC is clear that these brokers are not its agents and that it does not endorse their services. IPv4 Connect appears on that list under its operator, Brander Group. Its marketplace sells blocks at fixed prices instead of through auctions and includes a free blacklist report with every subnet. 

It also offers pre-approval assistance and fully managed transfers across ARIN, RIPE and APNIC, which it says typically take two to three weeks. A good broker also handles cleanup the registry won’t. That includes clearing old BGP announcements, stale route records and DNS entries before the block changes hands, so the space arrives ready to use.

What an APNIC Transfer Costs

There are two separate costs: the price you agree with the seller and APNIC’s own fees. The purchase price is set by the market and depends on block size and supply. For approved transfers inside the region, the recipient pays APNIC’s transfer fee, except NIR members. 

The fee is due before APNIC updates the Whois registration. On an outbound inter-RIR transfer, the APNIC account holder sending the space pays instead. APNIC has long calculated this fee as 20% of the annual fee for the block being transferred, as shown in its policy update briefing. 

Some transfers are exempt, so confirm the current figure on APNIC’s IPv4 Transfer Fees page before you budget. All APNIC fees are charged in Australian dollars. Membership is a recurring cost to plan for as well. Taking on more address space can raise your annual fees at the next renewal.

Moving Space Between Regions

Inter-RIR transfers let space cross between APNIC and other regional registries, such as ARIN and the RIPE NCC. APNIC only processes them when the counterpart registry has a compatible inter-RIR policy. Each side follows its own registry’s rules. An APNIC recipient still faces the 24-month plan test, while a recipient elsewhere meets its own registry’s conditions. 

When space leaves APNIC, linked objects such as route and domain objects are deleted from the APNIC Whois Database.

Due Diligence Before You Sign

A registry approval confirms the paperwork, not the quality of the block. Run these checks before committing funds:

  • Holder match. Confirm the Whois record names the seller as the current holder with no open dispute.
  • Delegation date. Rule out any 103/8 space still inside its five-year lock.
  • Reputation. Check the range against major IP blacklists so you don’t inherit someone else’s abuse history.
  • Routing hygiene. Make sure old announcements and route objects are cleared, then plan your own route objects and ROAs before you announce the block.
  • Payment protection. Use escrow or a structure that releases funds only after the registry records the transfer.

APNIC also publishes a public transfer log. It is a useful way to check a block’s recent history before you buy.

Treat the purchase with the same care you would give any security decision. You will be sharing network plans, invoices and account details with brokers and the registry, so follow the basics of how to keep your data safe when transferring large files.

Conclusion

APNIC’s transfer rules are strict but predictable. Buyers need an APNIC account and a credible 24-month plan. Sellers need clean title and a block outside the 103/8 lock. Both sides then work through MyAPNIC on a 30-day clock.

The smoothest deals settle the hard parts early. Get pre-approved first. Then verify the block’s history and reputation and budget for both the price and APNIC’s fees before you sign.

FAQ

Do I need an APNIC account to receive transferred IPv4? Yes. For transfers inside the region, the recipient must be a current APNIC account holder.

How long does the buyer have to accept a transfer? Thirty days from when the seller initiates it in MyAPNIC. After that, the request is cancelled.

Can I buy addresses from the 103/8 range? Only if at least five years have passed since APNIC originally delegated them.

Can IPv6 addresses be transferred in the APNIC region? APNIC only recognizes IPv6 transfers that result from a merger or acquisition.

Can AS numbers be transferred too? Yes. The recipient must meet APNIC’s normal criteria for being assigned an ASN.

item.title: Ukrainian Nefilim and Hive Affiliate Artem Stryzhak Jailed for 70 Months
item.description:
A Ukrainian man who helped carry out Nefilim and Hive ransomware attacks has been sentenced to 70 months in prison. Artem Stryzhak, 36, participated in operations that encrypted victims’ files and demanded payment for their recovery, including attacks against healthcare organisations during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The US Department of Justice announced the sentence on October 27. Stryzhak, formerly of Barcelona, was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the United States in April 2025. He pleaded guilty in December to two computer-crime conspiracy counts.

Paying for Access to Nefilim

Stryzhak joined Nefilim as an affiliate around June 2021, agreeing to give its administrators 20% of his ransom proceeds in exchange for access to the malware.

As Hackread.com reported following his guilty plea, the operation gave affiliates tools to research companies before attacking them. Stryzhak and his co-conspirators used public databases to examine prospective victims’ revenue, size and contact information.

They could then prepare a separate ransomware executable, decryption key and ransom note for each victim. The extortion continued after encryption, with threats to publish stolen information on Nefilim’s “Corporate Leaks” websites if companies refused to pay.

According to the DOJ’s press release, prosecutors described one June 2021 attack in which Stryzhak stole information from an oil and gas transportation company. About a week later, he created email addresses used in its ransom note. His participation in the Nefilim conspiracy continued until at least October 2021.

Hive Attacks Included Healthcare Victims

Stryzhak also became one of Hive’s earliest affiliates. He and his co-conspirators deployed its ransomware against seven victims, including law firms, a dental office and a healthcare provider.

During its investigation, the FBI supplied one of those victims with a decryption key, allowing it to recover encrypted files without paying. Authorities said Hive ransomware collectively attacked approximately 1,500 victims between June 2021 and January 2023, a group-wide figure, not Stryzhak’s individual victim count.

Investigators are still seeking his charged co-conspirator, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, whom prosecutors identify as a Nefilim administrator. The State Department is offering up to $11 million for information leading to his arrest or conviction, or establishing his location.

I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: ADEX: AI Involved in 52% of Detected Ad Fraud Schemes – Shopping Agents Could be Next
item.description:
LIMASSOL, Cyprus, October 27 2026 – AI played a significant role in 52% of Advertising fraud schemes identified by ADEX, a leading AI-powered traffic validation and anti-fraud ecosystem, between January and September 2026, according to the company’s new State of Ad Fraud 2026: ADEX Trust & Safety Report (PDF).

The findings are based on aggregated moderation data from eight advertising platforms using ADEX and cover 1.2 million campaigns and 4.9 million creatives.

Among AI-involved schemes, bots impersonating humans appeared in 64% fraud schemes, while cloned brands and fake endorsements featured in 53%. Deepfakes appeared in 11%. The categories overlap, as fraudulent schemes often tend to combine several AI-powered techniques.

The change AI brings about is fundamental though. A set of agents now stands in the place of a team of content makers, designers and developers. Fraud content today is super cheap to produce and even cheaper to scale.  And ADEX expects the next shift to take it a few levels up: in 2027, fraudsters may increasingly target the AI agents that browse websites, compare products, and make purchases on behalf of regular people.

The same old scam gets a shiny new wrapper

A typical fake investment campaign of only a couple of years ago usually meant a hastily assembled landing page, maybe a celebrity photograph paired with a fabricated quote. Behind, there was a small team working potential victims through private messages.

Today, AI can produce a polished imitation of a legitimate news outlet or financial institution that would look almost flawless to the naked eye. A chatbot can then handle conversations around the clock, responding fluently in the victim’s language. The quality can be so good even people well-versed in AI may not see it’s fake right away.

“The scheme itself has not changed in years: borrow a trusted face, promise big returns, move the victim into a private chat. What AI changed is the finish. The page looks real, the video looks real, and the person in the chat never sleeps and never makes a typo,” said Sergey Martianov, Chief Product Officer at ADEX

According to the report, brand cloning and fake endorsements appear across investment and blockchain scams, as well as fraudulent e-commerce stores. Attackers also imitate familiar technology brands to distribute fake security alerts.

AI has also accelerated the cycle of replacing fraudulent advertising materials. ADEX researchers observed cases in which revised versions of rejected campaigns returned within hours, sometimes on the same day. The company does not report a standard turnaround time, as it varies considerably between schemes.

The next target could be the AI doing your shopping

Online users delegate more and more tasks to AI assistants. That’s why ADEX expects fraudsters to adapt their tactics to an emerging new audience: machines who we allow to make decisions for us.

An example of such attack is prompt injection, where malicious instructions are embedded in content an AI agent consumes while performing a legitimate task.

These instructions could appear in invisible page elements, metadata, product images, or text addressed directly to AI assistants. Attackers could also serve different content to human visitors and AI agentsAI agents, adapting cloaking techniques already used to evade advertising moderation.

ADEX emphasizes that this is a forecast rather than an attack category currently measured in its moderation data. However, prompt-injection techniques are already documented in security research, and the company has previously examined how AI agents can be manipulated into delivering malicious content.

“In 2027, the most valuable user on the web may not be a person at all. If an agent is doing the shopping, someone will try to scam the agent. The industry needs to start checking ads for what they say to machines, too,” Martianov explained.

When a bot is also a legitimate customer

The expected growth of AI shopping agents presents another challenge for advertisers and platforms: distinguishing legitimate automated activity from malicious bots.

An AI assistant that compares prices or buys something for a real customer is doing a legitimate job, even if no human ever touches the website.

So the question isn’t “bot or human?” ADEX suggests asking three things instead. Can the visitor prove who it is? Does it behave the way its stated task says it should? And do its sessions end in something real, like a purchase or a booking? Platforms should also watch for websites that show AI agents one page and people another.

For advertisers, the to-do list is short. Keep an eye out for your brand in other people’s ads. Check where your clicks actually end up. And ask your technology partners a simple question: how do you tell a good agent from bad automation?

With AI now on both sides of the ad transaction, two questions matter more and more: who, or what, is making the decision, and what told it to?

The full findings are available in State of Ad Fraud 2026: ADEX Trust & Safety Report (PDF).

About ADEX

ADEX is a global anti-fraud and traffic-quality platform within AdTech Holding. It analyzes billions of impressions, clicks, and conversions, protecting AdTech products and partners from malware-driven and invalid traffic attacks.

Methodology

The report analyzes aggregated moderation and verification data from eight advertising platforms using ADEX, covering January through September 2026. AI involvement is calculated across distinct fraud schemes, rather than individual campaigns or accounts. Categories may overlap.

item.title: EMBRACE Flaws in 5 AI Coding Tools Enable Code Execution and File Theft
item.description:
Gal Weizman, a security researcher at cybersecurity company Forever Security, has identified a class of security flaws dubbed EMBRACE (EMbedded BRowser, trusted like a real one) in five AI coding tools.

Shared with Hackread.com ahead of its public release on October 29, the research identifies weaknesses in browser security controls integrated into Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Visual Studio Code (VS Code) and Claude Desktop.

The potential reach is noteworthy, with Forever Security estimating that hundreds of millions of developers and users could be affected since VS Code has around 40 million developers and Codex has more than 5 million weekly users.

Three Ways Embedded Browsers Can Be Abused

  • Cursor: Code execution. A malicious web page can exploit a communication bridge between Cursor’s embedded browser and its AI assistant to inject hidden instructions into the command composer. In testing, the assistant was manipulated into running an installation command that launched Calculator on the host system. The command initially hit a sandbox restriction, but the agent disabled the restriction and retried. The outcome depended on the model’s behavior.
  • GitHub Copilot: Address-bar spoofing. In version 1.1.27, a malicious page could change the URL displayed in Copilot’s browser preview without navigating to the claimed destination. The address bar and AI agent could therefore report github.com/login while displaying a page hosted by an attacker, creating an opportunity for phishing.
  • Codex, VS Code and Claude Desktop: File theft. Researchers found that local HTML files opened in these applications could access files beyond their intended project boundaries. In VS Code and Claude Desktop, web workers could bypass directory checks enforced on the main page. Codex lacked the relevant restriction, allowing direct file access. They demonstrated reading and exfiltrating files, including SSH keys, developer tokens and private documents.

Disclosure Timeline and Patch Status

Forever Security reported the Cursor flaw on September 10; it was patched on October 1. GitHub independently fixed the Copilot issue in version 1.1.29 on October 13, after the flaw was identified on September 26.

Researchers reported the Codex issue to OpenAI on July 27 and the VS Code issue to Microsoft on September 10. According to Weizman, neither issue had been patched at the time of publication.

The findings show how embedded browsers can expose developer systems to code execution, local file theft and address-bar spoofing when security boundaries are not properly enforced.

Hackread.com has previously reported on related risks, including attacks that use hidden website instructions to manipulate AI assistants and browser extensions to inject prompts into AI interfaces.

Businesses should note that a single developer endpoint running an affected tool could expose accessible SSH keys, cloud credentials, developer tokens and source code, or allow code execution on the host, depending on the product involved.

Forever Security advises organizations to identify these tools across developer endpoints and review the security controls governing their embedded browsers.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Binance Probes Suspected $5.8 Billion Crypto Hack, $3 Billion Frozen
item.description:
The cryprocurrency exchange Binance is investigating a suspected hack after billions of dollars moved from wallets associated with the exchange on October 29, 2026. Outside investigators have estimated the suspicious transfers at up to $5.8 billion, a figure that would make this the largest cryptocurrency theft publicly reported if confirmed.

The exchange has not confirmed that amount as stolen but confirmed that it was investigating the incident and assured customers that their funds were “completely safe.” Meanwhile, cryptocurrency issuers began freezing assets linked to the suspicious activity. 

Billions Moved Before Issuers Froze Assets

Blockchain investigators began examining large transfers involving several networks, with their estimates changing as additional transactions were identified.

Blockchain security company Blockaid said in a tweet it was investigating approximately $3.3 billion in suspicious outflows involving Ethereum, Arbitrum and Avalanche. Coinbase executive Conor Grogan placed the amount as high as $5.8 billion.

Those figures represent assessments made at different stages of the investigation. They should not be added together or treated as Binance’s final loss. 

Binance said in an October 30 update that approximately $3 billion had been verified as frozen. The exchange is working with law enforcement, token issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets. It reiterated that user funds are safe.

Freezing prevents affected tokens from being transferred under the issuer’s controls. It does not mean that the money has already been returned to Binance or establish how much the exchange will ultimately recover. 

How the Incident Unfolded

As investigators traced the transfers, Binance began issuing updates and stablecoin issuers froze funds. The timeline below follows those developments using Decrypt’s reporting and Unchained’s account of the announcements. The initial compromise may have occurred before the first recorded transfer.

Researchers Examine a Signed Wallet Delegation

Investigators examining the Ethereum transfers identified a signed authorization shortly before the funds moved. The authorization used EIP-7702, an Ethereum feature that allows a wallet to delegate functions to smart-contract code.

Phylax Systems founder Odysseas Lamtzidi described how that delegation could allow code to execute through the affected wallet and authorize further transfers. Decrypt reported that the authorization appeared three minutes and 24 seconds before the initial Ethereum transaction.

That finding could explain part of the transfer mechanism, but it does not explain how the required signature was obtained. The available reporting has not established whether an attacker stole signing credentials, compromised a signing system or persuaded someone to approve a malicious request. Nor does the use of EIP-7702 itself demonstrate a flaw in Ethereum. 

No Attacker Has Been Publicly Identified

Binance had not publicly attributed the incident to a named group in the statements reviewed for this report. The initial entry point, the people responsible and the full extent of access remained unknown. However, the incident comes about a month after Bitget reported a hack and suspected involvement by North Korea’s Lazarus Group.

CZ, who said he does not manage Binance anymore, wrote on X⁠ that the activity looked like a hack. Speaking as a shareholder, he said he expected all user funds to be fully covered. That was his expectation, separate from the exchange’s investigation and its own customer assurances. 

If the upper estimates are confirmed as stolen funds, the incident would exceed the approximately $1.5 billion Bybit theft in February 2025. However, the gross value moved, the amount frozen and the eventual unrecovered loss are different figures. None should be substituted for another while the investigation continues.

Binance.US separately said it was unaffected.

Binance Warns Customers About Unofficial Messages

Customers seeking information were directed to Binance’s official announcements. In its initial statement⁠, the exchange warned users about unofficial links, messages and requests for account information.

item.title: Binance Probes DevOps Engineer’s Hacked Laptop After $6.3B Theft
item.description:
Binance says its investigation into the $6.3 billion cryptocurrency hack and theft has identified several breach points, including a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop. Blockchain intelligence firms have attributed the hack to North Korean hackers tracked as TraderTraitor, associated with the Lazarus Group.

The October 30 updates provide the first explanation of how attackers reached Binance’s internal systems, alongside a commitment to cover all losses. However, withdrawals remain suspended while the exchange rebuilds security around the affected service.

Hackread.com’s earlier coverage reported outside estimates of up to $5.8 billion in suspicious transfers. Binance has since put the estimated impact at approximately $6.3 billion, making the incident substantially larger than the $1.5 billion Bybit theft in February 2025.

Compromised Laptop Was an Initial Finding

In its first detailed investigation update, Binance said a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop appeared to have allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. A DevOps engineer typically works on the infrastructure and processes used to deploy and operate software.

The attack resembles tactics used by North Korean hackers, who were observed in August 2026 using Ethereum-based dead drops in malicious npm packages to infect developers’ devices.

Binance said it had found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked. That distinction leaves open the possibility that attackers used access to internal systems to obtain authorized signatures for fraudulent transactions without taking the keys themselves. The exchange said it had revoked the affected address authorization and would publish a technical report after completing its investigation.

However, its later statement made clear that the laptop finding was not the complete explanation. Binance said investigators had identified additional breach points and were still gathering facts about what it described as a complex attack.

The exchange has not explained what those additional points were or how investigators compromised the engineer’s computer. The laptop should therefore be treated as an initial investigative finding, not a settled account of the entire attack.

“A compromised laptop may explain where an attack started, but it does not, on its own, explain how billions of dollars could leave an exchange,” argued Pieter Arntz, researcher at cybersecurity firm Malwarebytes.

“The real question is what allowed that initial foothold to become access to withdrawal systems – and which safeguards failed to stop unauthorized transactions. Until the technical investigation is complete, blaming a single laptop risks confusing the entry point with the full cause of the breach,” Pieter added.

Withdrawals Paused While Deposits Continue

Binance initially announced a precautionary suspension of deposits and withdrawals while it conducted security checks and worked with investigators.

A subsequent service update clarified that deposits were operating normally, while withdrawals remained paused during a security revamp of the withdrawal service and related addresses. Binance initially gave a 48-hour estimate for restoring withdrawals.

Its later announcement said it remained on track to resume the service within 45 hours of that update. That was an expected restoration window, not confirmation that withdrawals had reopened.

Binance Promises to Cover All Losses

Customers will not be required to absorb the losses, according to Binance. The exchange said it would use its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, together with company funds to cover the incident. It also promised an updated Proof of Reserves after remediation.

Binance’s verified announcements reviewed for this report put frozen assets at approximately $3 billion. Freezing restricts further transfers of affected assets, but does not mean the money has already been returned to the exchange.

The North Korea Connection

TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor with high confidence, citing blockchain evidence and intelligence obtained outside the blockchain.

The company calculated that approximately $6.36 billion left Binance wallets on ten networks, with most transfers occurring within about 20 minutes from 20.05 GMT on October 29. Its analysis identified preparation beginning at least 36 hours earlier, including funding through Tornado Cash and tests of attack code.

The firm said the combination of valid transactions on different networks pointed to compromised hot-wallet signing infrastructure. On Ethereum, the attacker also used EIP-7702 authorizations to make a Binance wallet execute attacker-controlled code and repeatedly transfer incoming funds.

TRM compared the preparation and signing patterns with earlier North Korea-linked thefts, including Bybit. Chainalysis CEO Jonathan Levin separately assessed that TraderTraitor was likely responsible. These are the firms’ attributions. Binance’s statements reviewed for this article have not named the attackers.

Binance has committed to releasing a full account of the incident. That report will need to explain how access to internal infrastructure translated into unauthorized withdrawals, what the additional breach points involved and which controls have been changed before customers can withdraw again.

item.title: Fake GitHub Repo Tricks AI Agents Into Installing SolanaCry Malware
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers at AIR Research Lab have discovered SolanaCry, a new malware delivered through a fake GitHub repository posing as a Solana starter kit. The repository can appear in AI coding agents‘ search results, leading them to follow instructions that install remote-access malware on developers’ Windows machines and potentially expose cryptocurrency wallets stored on those systems.

Malicious GitHub Repository Delivers NetSupport RAT

Rather than tricking developers into installing malicious software themselves, the attack targets AI agents through a malicious GitHub repository, SolanaUpdateTools/solana-starter-kit. Presented as an “open-source Solana dApp template with Anchor program, TypeScript client, and Next.js UI,” the repository was created in November 2025, had 286 stars when AIR examined it, and ranked first in search results for a Solana starter kit, researchers explained in a blog post shared with Hackread.com.

The README instructs AI agents to run a PowerShell command using Invoke-WebRequest and Invoke-Expression to download and execute a 21 MB dropper, indicator.ps1, directly in memory via fileless execution.

The script creates a hidden directory under the user’s local application data folder and extracts 14 files. These include 13 genuine, digitally signed NetSupport Manager components, including client32.exe and PCICL32.DLL, and an attacker-supplied configuration file, client32.ini.

NetSupport Manager is legitimate software that allows remote access to and management of computers. The attackers used it to connect to infected machines through a server at maxwintodaybtc.com:443. Its configuration hides notifications and disconnect options from users, sends a check-in signal every 60 seconds, and allows connections from any IP address.

The malware also adds client32.exe to the Windows Registry so that it starts automatically whenever the user logs in. It not only launches the program but also clears the history of commands entered through the Windows Run dialog and deletes the PowerShell script used to install the malware.

Links to Earlier Malware Campaigns

AIR Research Lab identified similarities between this campaign and earlier malware activity. The RADIUSSecret value inside client32.ini matches signature data that eSentire uses to identify EVALUSION, a cluster known for distributing NetSupport through ClickFix campaigns. This provides a possible link to previously tracked activity, although the match alone does not confirm who operated the campaign, researchers noted.

The installation command also follows the same pattern as one used in an October 2025 campaign documented by Fortian. That campaign used fake TradingView AI-signal content and a malicious GitHub repository to target cryptocurrency traders. The domain developer-update.app was registered on October 20, 2025, while the recovered payload was archived on November 22 that year, according to AIR’s report.

The attack follows a pattern covered in earlier Hackread.com reporting. In June 2026, researchers demonstrated Agentjacking attacks that trick AI coding agents into executing commands. In July, a GitLost prompt injection flaw showed how a crafted GitHub issue could trick an AI agent into exposing private repository data.

The SolanaCry findings also come as Binance investigates a DevOps engineer’s hacked laptop following its $6.3 billion theft, showing why developers’ computers are valuable targets for attackers seeking access to cryptocurrency infrastructure.

Given these recurring incidents, developers should exercise caution and check repository owners and installation instructions before allowing coding agents to execute commands or install dependencies from untrusted sources.

item.title: TeamViewer Vulnerability Lets Attackers Run Code on IT Support Staff’s PCs
item.description:
A vulnerability in TeamViewer could let attackers run code on an IT support technician’s computer when the technician connected to an attacker-controlled device. Once the remote session was established, the attack required no further clicks or theft of the technician’s password.

The now-patched vulnerability affected TeamViewer, a remote-access tool commonly used by corporate help desks to troubleshoot employees’ devices.

Cybersecurity firm Remedio discovered the flaw and shared details of the investigation with Hackread.com. According to Remedio researcher Omri Dar, on an unpatched system, the attack works as soon as the technician accepts the incoming connection.

How the Integer Overflow Works

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111585, targets TeamViewer’s screen decompression component. When a session opens, the host transmits screen dimensions called DisplayParams to the viewer. TeamViewer processes these values inside a memory buffer named CBitmapBuffer, where incoming screen updates are decompressed.

The problem lies in how TeamViewer calculates the memory needed to process incoming screen images. The buffer constructor uses 32-bit multiplication to calculate the required memory, but by sending unusually large screen dimensions, such as 32,768 by 32,768 pixels, an attacker can make the calculation produce an incorrect result.

TeamViewer then allocates only around 4 MB of memory but continues processing the image as if it had enough space for the full dimensions. The decoder then checks incoming data against the declared screen dimensions rather than the actual allocated memory. This allows decompressed pixel data to overwrite adjacent heap memory, creating a heap-based buffer overflow.

Remedio demonstrated that the memory corruption could be used to bypass Data Execution Prevention (DEP) and Control Flow Guard (CFG), redirect execution to WinExec and run attacker-controlled code on the technician’s computer.

“Exploitation requires a user to establish a remote-control session to an attacker-controlled or compromised host,” TeamViewer noted.

TeamViewer Releases Security Updates

Remedio notified TeamViewer’s Product Security team about the flaw on August 14, 2026. TeamViewer confirmed the issue on October 22, assigning it CVE-2026-111585 with a CVSS score of 8.8 (Severity: High).

The fix arrived on October 27 in version 15.83. TeamViewer’s security bulletin also covers two other flaws: CVE-2026-92372, which affects screen-image decoding on Linux and macOS, and CVE-2026-92374, which could allow local attackers to gain root privileges on macOS. They carry CVSS scores of 8.8 and 7.8, respectively.

TeamViewer said it had found no evidence of the flaws being exploited in the wild and advised users to update to the latest version.

Hackread.com has previously reported on attacks in which cybercriminals abused TeamViewer to access company systems. However, this latest discovery is different, as it involves a flaw in TeamViewer itself that allows a computer receiving technical support to attack the technician’s machine.

Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience…
